title: 3Sum: sort + fix one + two-pointer scan, skip duplicates.
shortTitle: 3Sum: Sort + Fix One + Two-Pointer, Skip Duplicates
keyPoints: Sort the array first, then fix one element and use two pointers on the remaining sorted range to find pairs completing the triple.
Skip duplicates at three points: the fixed element, the left pointer after a match, and the right pointer after a match.
Overall time is O(n squared) because the O(n log n) sort is dominated by the nested two-pointer scan.
Early exit: once the fixed element exceeds zero (when target is zero), no triple can sum to zero because the remaining elements are all larger.
For BigDecimal amounts, use compareTo for sum comparison and duplicate checks so scale differences do not create spurious distinct values.
The naive triple nested loop is O(n cubed); sort plus two-pointer reduces it to O(n squared) with O(1) extra space.

s1_definition.oneliner: Sort, fix one element, then two-pointer the rest inward, skipping duplicates to keep triples unique.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **3Sum** – find all unique triples in an array that sum to a target, typically zero.
- **Sort first** – sorting enables both the two-pointer pair search and easy duplicate skipping.
- **Fix one, scan two** – the outer loop fixes the first element; left and right pointers scan the remaining range.
- **Duplicate skipping** – three skip points: the fixed element, left after a match, right after a match.
- **Complexity** – O(n squared) time, O(1) extra space beyond the output.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants to find every group of three transactions on Rajesh's account that net to zero, meaning they cancel out, because such offsetting triples can signal wash-trading. First the amounts are sorted. Then a clerk fixes one amount and uses two fingers on the rest of the sorted list, one at the low end and one at the high end, moving them toward each other: if the three add to more than zero the high finger steps down, if less the low finger steps up, and if exactly zero the triple is recorded. Duplicate amounts are skipped so the same triple is never reported twice.

sections.s6_takeaway:
3Sum finds all unique triples that sum to a target, usually zero, and the standard solution is sort plus two-pointer. I sort the array first, which lets me use the two-pointer technique: for each fixed first element I put a left pointer just after it and a right pointer at the end, and I move them inward based on the sum. Sorting is O(n log n) and the nested scan is O(n squared), so the whole thing is O(n squared), which is the accepted optimal and far better than the O(n cubed) brute force.

The part I am most careful about is skipping duplicates at three points: skip a fixed element equal to the previous one, and after recording a triple advance the left pointer past equal values and the right pointer past equal values. Those three skips are what keep the triples unique, and missing any of them produces repeated triples in the output.

I also use the early-exit optimisation: because the array is sorted, once the fixed element exceeds zero no triple can sum to zero, so I break out of the outer loop. For banking amounts I use BigDecimal with compareTo for both the sum comparison and the duplicate checks, so scale differences do not create spurious distinct values, and I sort a copy to leave the caller's array untouched.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India, I used this in wash-trade surveillance to find all unique sets of three transactions whose signed amounts net to zero, because offsetting triples where credits and debits cancel can indicate faked activity. Days contain duplicate amounts, so the three duplicate-skips ensure each offsetting triple is reported exactly once.

Remember one sentence: sort the array, fix one element, two-pointer the rest inward, and skip duplicates at three points to get all unique triples in O(n squared).
